name: prqlc
why: A pipelined query language that compiles to SQL is a genuinely different way to think about queries.

brief.what_it_is: PRQL (Pipelined Relational Query Language, pronounced 'Prequel') is a language for transforming data, described by its authors as a simple, powerful, pipelined SQL replacement. You write a query as a linear list of transformations (from, filter, derive, group, aggregate, sort, take, join, select), and the compiler turns it into SQL for a chosen database dialect. The tool in this entry is prqlc, the Rust compiler and CLI, which takes PRQL text and emits SQL; it can also format and annotate PRQL queries. Bindings exist for Python (prqlc-python, pyprql), JavaScript (prqlc-js) and R.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames PRQL as a readable alternative to SQL that keeps SQL's explicit, declarative style but forms a logical pipeline and supports variables and functions. The homepage says it was originally designed for analytical queries, emphasizing data transformations, development speed and readability.
brief.how_it_works: Each line of a PRQL query transforms the result of the line before it, so the query reads top to bottom starting from the table. The compiler, written in Rust, translates the pipeline into SQL for the target dialect, and s-strings let you embed raw SQL where PRQL has no equivalent. The homepage example shows 'filter' placed both before and after an aggregation, which PRQL turns into WHERE and HAVING clauses.

brief.install_notes: Install with cargo, brew or winget as listed on the homepage; no accounts, runtimes beyond what each package manager needs, or hardware are mentioned. The README says the project can be built 'in a couple of commands' and points to a development doc (prql-lang.org/book/project/contributing/development.html) for build details, which I did not fetch. Integrations like the VS Code extension, Jupyter magic, DuckDB extension and QStudio are separate installs.
brief.standout: Compared with other SQL alternatives, the pipeline-of-transformations model means a query is always valid when you comment out one line, which the homepage calls out for analysts exploring data. It compiles to many SQL dialects rather than replacing a single database, and it is pitched as an open standard-like target that tools can read and write.
brief.status: quiet. The GitHub README has a 'Current Status - July 2026' section saying development has slowed while the maintainers decide how to build a new resolver, and that the project still has bugs and missing features. Integrations and a CI badge are present, but I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so I can't confirm recent activity beyond that status note.
brief.caveats: The README says PRQL 'still has some bugs and some missing features' and is 'probably only ready to be rolled out to non-technical teams for fairly simple queries.' Module/multi-file support is experimental, and the handling of window functions outside a window transform is listed as an open question. Type checking, error messages and column lineage are marked 'in progress' on the homepage. Java, C, C++, Elixir, .NET and PHP bindings are unsupported or nascent. Its focus is analytical queries; it de-emphasizes inserts and transactions. The homepage says the project is open-source and will never have a commercial product; I did not see a license name in what I fetched.
quotes: PRQL is a modern language for transforming data — a simple, powerful, pipelined SQL replacement.
Each line of the query is a transformation of the previous line’s result.
PRQL still has some bugs and some missing features, and is probably only ready to be rolled out to non-technical teams for fairly simple queries.
It can be used with any database that uses SQL, since it compiles to SQL.
